clue.text: Pet at the chemist’s, the old story

blocks.note: puss = a pet cat
Boots is the big British chain of chemist's shops, so 'at the chemist's' = IN BOOTS

explanation.surface: Someone spots a cat wandering around a pharmacy and recognises a familiar tale.
explanation.walkthrough: Boots is Britain's best-known high-street chemist, which is the whole trick: a cat at the chemist's is literally a puss in Boots.
explanation.definitionFit: Puss in Boots is an old fairy tale about a clever cat.

clue.text: Pound and a penny: let’s start to eat out

definitions.note: the clue gives the verb (what the tool does); the answer is the tool that pounds

indicators.note: the start of 'eat' is its first letter
'out' as in wild or disordered: the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: p = penny
anagram fodder
first letter of eat, added to the fodder

explanation.surface: Someone counting coins announces it is time to go out for a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pound' looks like money next to 'a penny', but it is the verb: a pestle is what you pound with in a mortar.
explanation.definitionFit: A pestle is the club-shaped tool used to pound things in a mortar.

clue.text: In great misery, God’s help found so transforming

indicators.note: the letters are transformed into a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 15 letters

explanation.surface: A believer in deep despair finds that divine help changed everything.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a conversion story, which suits an answer taken from Bunyan's The Pilgrim's Progress, where Christian sinks into the Slough of Despond.
explanation.definitionFit: The Slough of Despond, a bog in The Pilgrim's Progress, is proverbial for a state of deep despair.

clue.text: Better holding is made up

indicators.note: the outer word holds the other inside it

blocks.note: bettered = improved
used as it stands, placed inside IMPROV…ED

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a better-looking plot of land has been invented.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better' has to be read as a past tense, bettered, to give IMPROVED; 'made up' means invented on the spot, not reconciled.
explanation.definitionFit: Improvised means made up on the spot, without preparation.

clue.text: Bowled, do you agree? Not if these result

definitions.note: an allusive definition: the runs that come about when the ball beats the bat but not the stumps

blocks.note: b = bowled on a cricket scorecard
the answer to 'do you agree?'

explanation.surface: A cricketer asks whether everyone agrees he was bowled, only to be told otherwise.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, byes are runs scored when the ball passes the batter and the wicketkeeper without touching anything; if the ball had hit the stumps the batter would be bowled, so no byes.
explanation.definitionFit: Byes are runs taken when the bowled ball misses bat and stumps alike, the opposite of being bowled.

clue.text: Compose in too ornate a style, but finished properly, we hear

definitions.text: Compose in too ornate a style

indicators.note: the second part is what we hear, not what is written

blocks.note: the game is over = finished
right = properly, said the same as WRITE

explanation.surface: A writer is told the prose is too flowery, though at least it was completed correctly.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pretends to be a critic's verdict, which is why the definition and the wordplay both sound like comments on the same piece of writing.
explanation.definitionFit: To overwrite is to write in an overly elaborate, ornate style.

clue.text: Not the usual way to classify

blocks.note: St = street, a way
to range = to arrange in ranks or classes

explanation.surface: Someone objects to an unconventional method of sorting things.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one phrase, 'the usual way to classify', so the split after 'usual' is hard to see; 'way' is a street, abbreviated ST.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym phrased as a negative: whatever departs from the usual is odd or unfamiliar.

clue.text: He directed men and boys to conserve energy source first

indicators.note: SONS keeps the other letters inside it
the source comes first, then the energy

blocks.note: OR = other ranks, ordinary soldiers
boys = sons; this is the outer word
a well is a source of water
E = energy, after WELL because the source comes first

explanation.surface: A plea to men and boys to save power by using the main supply first.
explanation.walkthrough: OR for 'men' is a crossword staple: other ranks. 'Source first' fixes the order, WELL then E, before SONS closes around the pair.
explanation.definitionFit: Orson Welles directed Citizen Kane, among other films.

clue.text: Don’t hold back Lady Macbeth’s feeling about her spot?

definitions.text: Lady Macbeth’s feeling about her spot?

blocks.note: the plain meaning: say it, speak up

blocks.clueFragment: Lady Macbeth’s feeling about her spot?
blocks.note: she cries 'Out, damned spot!', so she wants it out

explanation.surface: A confidant urges Lady Macbeth to confess what she really feels about that bloodstain.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half leans on the sleepwalking scene in Macbeth, where Lady Macbeth scrubs at imagined blood crying 'Out, damned spot!'; the question mark flags the whimsy.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Out with it!' urges someone to stop holding back and say what they mean.

clue.text: Big band music be hanged

blocks.note: the jazz style of the big bands
the fate of a man on the gallows, left dangling

explanation.surface: Someone bursts out with a grumpy dismissal of big band music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Be hanged' reads as a curse on the music, but it is the second definition: to swing for a crime is to be hanged for it.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the jazz of Goodman and Basie in the 1930s and 40s; the other is old slang for dangling from the gallows, as in 'he'll swing for it'.

clue.text: Most precise projectile fired into sniper’s lair

indicators.note: one piece is shot into the middle of the other

blocks.note: a sniper's nest; this is the outer word
an arrow is a projectile, placed inside N…EST

explanation.surface: A marksman's shot, aimed with great accuracy, lands in an enemy sniper's hide.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all shooting, so 'Most precise' reads as praise for the shot rather than the definition, as in the narrowest of margins.
explanation.definitionFit: Narrowest can mean most exact or strict, as in the narrowest interpretation.

clue.text: Dangerous activity for the most gentlemanly competitor

blocks.note: bungee jumping, BASE jumping and the like
a good sport plays fair; the most extreme one is the most gentlemanly

explanation.surface: A risky pastime is suggested as fit only for the most courteous of rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads 'sport' as a person, as in 'be a sport', and 'extreme' as the superlative.
explanation.definitionFit: An extreme sport is a high-risk activity such as skydiving or free climbing.

clue.text: Brochure made from the tiniest bit of tree?

blocks.note: a printed handout
botanically, one small division of a compound leaf

explanation.surface: Someone muses on how little of a tree goes into making a pamphlet.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests paper made from wood pulp; the second sense is botanical, a leaflet being a little leaf, and the question mark flags the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: A leaflet is a small printed sheet or brochure handed out to people.

clue.text: Oozing round one side of lid, about to drop off

indicators.note: the outer word goes round the other
one edge of 'lid', its first letter

blocks.note: seepy = oozing; this is the outer word
first letter of lid, placed inside S…EEPY

explanation.surface: Something sticky is seeping round the edge of a lid that is about to fall off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drop off' pretends to be about the lid falling; in the definition it means nodding off to sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleepy describes someone about to drop off to sleep.

clue.text: Brandish gun, a fine specimen

blocks.note: to brandish something is to show it off
piece = a gun, in slang

explanation.surface: Someone waves a firearm about, admiring it as a beautiful example of its kind.
explanation.walkthrough: PIECE for gun is American gangster slang; the surface keeps the weapon in view so 'fine specimen' reads as praise for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A showpiece is an outstanding example, one fit to be put on display.

clue.text: In brief ceremony almost nothing about one could be more richly stylish

indicators.note: cut short: the last letter goes
not quite all of the word
goes around the next piece

blocks.note: RITE without its last letter
ZERO without its last letter; the outer piece
I = one, placed inside Z…ER

explanation.surface: A pared-down ceremony, with next to nothing spent on anyone, might turn out more elegant.
explanation.walkthrough: RITZY comes from the Ritz hotels, a byword for luxury; two different words for 'shortened' do the trimming here.
explanation.definitionFit: Ritzy means luxuriously smart, so ritzier is more richly stylish.

clue.text: Plague is to lessen after time

indicators.note: the lessening comes after the time

blocks.note: t = time
to ease pain is to lessen it

explanation.surface: A statement that an epidemic fades as time passes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plague' looks like the disease, a noun; here it is the verb, to pester someone.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Plague' in its verb sense, to pester persistently, is what a tormenting sibling does with jibes.

clue.text: Diver circles a good lake

indicators.note: the diver goes round the other letters

blocks.note: a loon is a diving bird; this is the outer word
used as it stands
g = good, placed with A inside L…OON

explanation.surface: A scuba diver swims in circles around a pleasant lake.
explanation.walkthrough: The diver is a bird: the loon, called a diver in Britain, which is why it circles rather than dives.
explanation.definitionFit: A lagoon is a stretch of shallow water cut off from the sea, a kind of lake.

clue.text: Chief bird showing off

blocks.note: a swan is a bird
a king is a chief

explanation.surface: The dominant bird in a flock struts about displaying itself.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces go in the other order from the clue: bird first, then chief, as in 'the swan king'. To swank is British for to show off.
explanation.definitionFit: Swanking is British slang for showing off or swaggering.

clue.text: Cover where some dogs like to sprawl

definitions.text: where some dogs like to sprawl

blocks.note: to extend across part of something, as roof tiles do

blocks.clueFragment: where some dogs like to sprawl
blocks.note: a lapdog likes to lie over a lap

explanation.surface: A dog blanket placed where pets like to stretch out.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the answer as OVER LAP, where small dogs love to drape themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: To overlap something is to extend over and partly cover it.

clue.text: Observe diluted gallon coming to the boil

blocks.note: to observe is to see
diluted = thinned, thin
g = gallon

explanation.surface: Someone watches a watered-down gallon of liquid heat up on the stove.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diluted gallon' reads as one thing, but it splits into THIN and the abbreviation G.
explanation.definitionFit: Seething describes liquid bubbling as it comes to the boil, and by extension a person fuming.

clue.text: Don’t delay rushed, curt thank-you note?

blocks.note: the proverb urging you to act now
read as a telegram: a clipped apology for haste, then thanks for the gift

explanation.surface: Someone dashing off a terse note of thanks, with no time to linger.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the second half as a telegram: 'No time. Like the present.' It is short because the writer is rushed, and it thanks the giver for a present.
explanation.definitionFit: 'There's no time like the present' is the saying that tells you not to put things off.

clue.text: Gang regularly taken in school run a pain

indicators.note: every other letter of 'gang'
one piece is taken inside the others

blocks.note: a school of whales is also a pod
second and fourth letters of gAnG, placed after POD
r = run, in cricket scoring
used as it stands

explanation.surface: A gang is regularly picked up during the school run, and it is a nuisance.
explanation.walkthrough: The school run, driving children to school, is the obvious reading, but 'school' here is a group of whales and 'a pain' holds the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Podagra is gout, especially in the big toe, a painful condition.

clue.text: Unbalanced, I am helped to avoid area

indicators.note: the area is left out of the word

blocks.note: 'I am' is formally 'one is', contracted to ONE'S
helped = aided
a = area; taken out of AIDED to leave IDED

explanation.surface: Someone admits to being lopsided, having been helped to steer clear of a place.
explanation.walkthrough: The formal pronoun 'one' stands for 'I', so 'I am' becomes 'one is', written ONE'S.
explanation.definitionFit: Used of a contest or argument, both describe something tilted heavily in one direction.

clue.text: Wrongly suggesting eastern and southern area of US?

definitions.text: Wrongly suggesting eastern and southern area of US?

blocks.note: read the answer as 'middle of WEST': the middle letters of WEST are E and S, eastern and southern
the real meaning: a region of the United States, nowhere near the east or south

explanation.surface: A remark that a US region's name gives a misleading idea of where it is.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as MID WEST and it describes the middle of the word WEST, which is E and S; the region itself is in the north-central United States.
explanation.definitionFit: The Midwest is the region of the north-central United States, including states such as Ohio, Illinois and Iowa.

clue.text: Muslim hermit is around after a month

indicators.note: the second piece comes after the month

blocks.note: Mar = March
around = about

explanation.surface: A holy recluse is said to be back in the area after a month away.
explanation.walkthrough: A marabout is a Muslim holy man or hermit in North and West Africa; the word is also the name of a stork.
explanation.definitionFit: A marabout is a Muslim holy man or hermit, especially in North Africa.

clue.text: Wife no longer referred to as aroused

blocks.note: an ex-wife is a wife no longer
cited = referred to

explanation.surface: A former wife, once called passionate, is no longer described that way.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a marriage gone cold; the definition is at the end, and 'as' only links it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe feelings or passions that have been stirred up.

clue.text: Senior commander arrests one very unmilitary

indicators.note: the commander holds the others captive inside

blocks.note: CIC = commander-in-chief; this is the outer word
I = one
v = very; with I, placed inside C…IC

explanation.surface: A top general detains a soldier who is not soldierly enough.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all army, which hides that the definition means civilian, the opposite of military.
explanation.definitionFit: Civic means relating to citizens and civil life, not the military.

clue.text: Convertible option coming from the leader

blocks.note: a soft-top car driven with its roof folded away
management jargon for decisions imposed from above

explanation.surface: A choice of open-top car handed down by the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is the car's roof folded back; the second is management jargon for decisions imposed from above.
explanation.definitionFit: Top-down describes both an open convertible and control imposed by the leadership.

clue.text: Not quite get the better of author, more than satisfied with extravagant fee

definitions.note: an adjective phrase: overcompensated means paid with an extravagant fee

indicators.note: the last letter is dropped

blocks.clueFragment: Not quite get the better of
blocks.note: OVERCOME without its last letter
to pen is to write, author
sated = filled beyond satisfaction

explanation.surface: A writer nearly beaten, yet more than pleased with a lavish payment.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition hides at the end after a long run of wordplay; 'author' is a verb here, to pen.
explanation.definitionFit: Overcompensated means paid too much, given an extravagant fee.

clue.text: Overcharge for plant

blocks.note: informal British verb for charging a customer too much
a grass-like plant of marshes, once used for floor mats and candle wicks

explanation.surface: A garden centre charges too much for a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang, to rush a customer is to overcharge them: 'How much did they rush you for that?'
explanation.definitionFit: Rush means both to overcharge and a grass-like marsh plant.

clue.text: Find one’s about to enter port

indicators.note: the pieces go inside the port

blocks.note: Dover, the English Channel port; this is the outer word
one's = I'S, I being one
c = circa, about; with IS, placed inside D…OVER

explanation.surface: A traveller learns they are about to arrive at the harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to' reads as 'on the point of', but 'about' is C (circa) and 'to enter' is the instruction. Dover is England's main Channel port.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to come upon something for the first time, as explorers or scientists do.

clue.text: Tin with dreadful soup — just one star

indicators.note: the soup is in a dreadful state: its letters are jumbled

blocks.note: a tin is a can
SOUP rearranged

explanation.surface: A restaurant review of tinned soup so bad it earns a single star.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a one-star review of canned soup; the star is real, Canopus, the second-brightest in the night sky.
explanation.definitionFit: Canopus is a single star, the brightest in the constellation Carina.

clue.text: Be in charge and come down to speak

indicators.note: the word is spoken, so only its sound counts

blocks.note: what the weather does when it comes down, said aloud

explanation.surface: A leader is urged to take control and come downstairs to address the people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come down' is weather: rain falls, and rain is said the same as reign.
explanation.definitionFit: What a monarch does on the throne, extended to anyone who holds sway.

clue.text: Tutor’s work with small son on sci-fi writer

indicators.note: the small son comes on after the writer

blocks.note: to go is to work, function
Jules Verne, author of Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea
s = small
s = son

explanation.surface: A tutor's own writing, done with a young boy, builds on a science-fiction author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tutor's work' reads as one phrase, but the definition is just 'Tutor', with 's as 'is'; 'work' is GO, as in 'does it go?'
explanation.definitionFit: A governess is a woman employed to tutor children in a private household.

clue.text: In dispute, referee’s assistant intended to ignore fine

definitions.note: the answer is a noun; 'at variance' means in dispute

indicators.note: the fine is left out of the word

blocks.note: VAR = video assistant referee, in football
one's intended is one's fiancé
f = fine; taken out of FIANCE to leave IANCE

explanation.surface: In a row over a match, the video referee meant to let a penalty go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Intended' reads as 'meant', but it is a noun: one's intended, a fiancé. VAR is football's video assistant referee.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'at variance with' describes parties who disagree, so the noun stands for a state of dispute.

clue.text: Philosopher isn’t tweeting nonsense

indicators.note: the letters make nonsense and must be rearranged

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

explanation.surface: A great thinker declines to post rubbish on social media.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is apt: Wittgenstein famously said that whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.
explanation.definitionFit: Ludwig Wittgenstein was an Austrian-British philosopher of language and logic.

clue.text: Entering hotel, putting specs and card in receptacle

indicators.note: 'putting' something somewhere is placing it, so the specs and card are placed as the next word directs
'in' names where they go: inside the receptacle, whose letters wrap round them

blocks.note: a bin is a receptacle; this is the outer word
two round lenses look like OO
a king is a playing card; with OO, placed inside B…IN

explanation.surface: Checking in at a hotel, a guest drops glasses and a key card into a tray.
explanation.walkthrough: Specs as OO is visual: a pair of spectacles looks like two Os side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Booking in means registering on arrival at a hotel.

clue.text: Check competitiveness, not initially courteous behaviour

indicators.note: 'initially' means at the start, so 'not initially' tells you to lose the word's opening letter

blocks.note: ch = check, in chess notation
RIVALRY without its first letter

explanation.surface: Keeping rivalry in check is described as the gentlemanly way to behave.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface frames chivalry as the opposite of rivalry, yet it is built from rivalry with its head cut off.
explanation.definitionFit: Chivalry is courteous, gallant behaviour, especially towards women.

clue.text: Swimmer’s blue with cold penetrating

indicators.note: the cold goes into the other word

blocks.note: feeling blue = sad; this is the outer word
c = cold, on taps; placed inside S…AD

explanation.surface: A swimmer turns blue as the cold water gets through to them.
explanation.walkthrough: The swimmer is a fish: the scad, or horse mackerel; 'Swimmer's' means 'Swimmer is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A scad is a fish, also called a horse mackerel.

clue.text: Applause welcoming a huge success for racing driver

indicators.note: the applause takes the success into its arms

blocks.note: a cheer is applause; this is the outer word
a riot = a huge success, as in 'the show was a riot'; placed inside CH…EER

explanation.surface: A crowd cheers a Formula One winner after a triumphant race.
explanation.walkthrough: The racing driver is ancient: a charioteer drove in chariot races, not Grand Prix.
explanation.definitionFit: A charioteer drove a chariot, often in races.

clue.text: Buried away from home, with no confirmation of age

indicators.note: the home letters are taken away

blocks.note: buried under, swamped, as in 'buried in work'
at home = in; taken off the front of INUNDATED

explanation.surface: Someone laid to rest abroad, with no proof of how old they were.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a grave, but 'buried' means swamped, as with emails: inundated.
explanation.definitionFit: Something undated bears no date, so its age is unconfirmed.

clue.text: Supernatural creature I found in gutter, a source of irritation

indicators.note: the creature and I are found inside the gutter

blocks.note: a ditch is a gutter; this is the outer word
a hob is a goblin or sprite
used as it stands; with HOB, placed inside D…ITCH

explanation.surface: Someone finds a goblin lurking in the drain, which is annoying.
explanation.walkthrough: Dhobi itch is a fungal skin rash of the tropics, named after the dhobi, an Indian washerman.
explanation.definitionFit: Dhobi itch is an itchy fungal skin infection, a literal source of irritation.

clue.text: Plant college in favoured area

indicators.note: the college goes inside the other letters

blocks.note: a pet project is a favoured one
uni = university
a = area; PET + A wrap round UNI

explanation.surface: A university is sited in a popular part of town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like a verb, to site a college; it is the definition, a flower.
explanation.definitionFit: The petunia is a garden plant with trumpet-shaped flowers.

clue.text: Taking principal piece last, fastening up paraphernalia

indicators.note: the first letter is moved to the end

blocks.note: strapping up = fastening

explanation.surface: Someone packs the most important item last while buckling up a bag of gear.
explanation.walkthrough: The instruction comes first and sounds like packing advice; it tells you to move the leading S of STRAPPING to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Trappings are the accessories and outward trimmings that go with something.

clue.text: Novel approach, collecting unknown religious literature

indicators.note: a new arrangement of the letters
the fodder takes in the unknown

blocks.note: anagram fodder
y = an unknown in algebra, collected into the fodder

explanation.surface: A fresh take on gathering obscure sacred writings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book, fitting 'literature', but it is the anagram indicator; X, Y and Z are the algebraic unknowns.
explanation.definitionFit: The Apocrypha are biblical writings not accepted into the canon.

clue.text: A quiet reputation not at first given to dwarfs’ leader, Bashful

indicators.note: the first letter is dropped
the first letter of 'dwarfs'

blocks.note: used as it stands
sh! = be quiet
FAME without its first letter
first letter of dwarfs

explanation.surface: Snow White's shy dwarf gets a quiet reputation among the others.
explanation.walkthrough: Bashful is one of Disney's seven dwarfs, so the surface tempts you to look for a dwarf; the name is the definition, meaning embarrassed.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashamed is close to bashful: embarrassed and self-conscious.

clue.text: Parliament put in a fix by a rigged photo: now there’s a story

indicators.note: the photo is faked, its letters rearranged
beside, next to the other pieces

blocks.note: the House of Commons
A PHOTO rearranged
to corner someone is to put them in a fix

explanation.surface: Parliament is embarrassed by a doctored photograph, and the press has a scandal.

clue.text: Counter Reformation composer shortly to meet his monarch

indicators.note: cut short: the last letter goes

blocks.note: Thomas TALLIS, Tudor composer, without his last letter
ER = Elizabeth Regina, Queen Elizabeth I, whom Tallis served

explanation.surface: A composer of the Counter-Reformation is briefly presented to his sovereign.

clue.text: Second demonstrator’s moral lesson

blocks.note: one who proves, demonstrates
B is second, after A

explanation.surface: A second teacher is giving a lesson in ethics.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces go in the other order from the clue; 'demonstrator' looks like a protester but is one who demonstrates, a prover.
explanation.definitionFit: A proverb is a short saying carrying a moral lesson.

clue.text: Law on drink performs badly

blocks.note: an act of parliament is a law
to sup is to drink

explanation.surface: Legislation on alcohol is working poorly.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a licensing law failing; 'acts up' is a machine or a child misbehaving.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that acts up malfunctions or behaves badly.

clue.text: Settle to repair what’s unravelling?

blocks.note: to settle a bill or pay costs
an invented word: the prefix that undoes, as in de-ice, plus the word for unravelling

explanation.surface: Someone thinks about how to mend a fraying garment.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half splits the answer as DE + FRAY, like de-ice or de-frost; the question mark flags the invented word.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal word used almost only of expenses: paying a bill is settling it.

clue.text: Look into swimming costume, a bit short for very large figures

indicators.note: the look goes into the costume
the costume loses its last letter

blocks.note: COSSIE, British and Australian slang for a swimsuit, without its last letter; the outer word

clue.text: Sort of love some tea with meals provided

definitions.note: the answer is the word that goes with 'love' in 'cupboard love'

blocks.note: a cup of tea
board = meals provided, as in bed and board

explanation.surface: Affection for whoever serves the tea and dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: Cupboard love is affection shown for what you can get, like a cat loving whoever feeds it, which is exactly the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Cupboard love is affection shown only in hope of reward, such as food.

clue.text: Blokes’ fortune in type of gas

indicators.note: the fortune goes inside the gas

blocks.note: CS gas, a tear gas; this is the outer word
hap = luck, fortune; placed inside C…S

explanation.surface: Some men's wealth is tied up in industrial gas.
explanation.walkthrough: CS gas is the tear gas used in riot control; 'hap' is an old word for chance, as in hapless.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaps and blokes are both British words for men.

clue.text: Following collapse close crew’s quarters

indicators.note: the word falls apart and its letters are rearranged

blocks.note: f = following, as in p. 5f
CLOSE rearranged

explanation.surface: After a building falls down, the sailors' living area is shut.
explanation.walkthrough: The fo'c'sle, short for forecastle, is the front of a ship where the crew traditionally lived.
explanation.definitionFit: The fo'c'sle is the forward part of a ship, where the crew's quarters were.

clue.text: Sparingly eat a measure of grain

blocks.note: to nibble at food like a bird
an old dry measure, a quarter of a bushel

explanation.surface: Advice to eat just a little grain.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a bird pecking at grain; both halves are definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: To peck is to eat in small bites, and a peck is a dry measure of grain.

clue.text: Loaded information at end of magazine column

indicators.note: the last letter of 'magazine'

blocks.note: spin = information slanted to favour one side
last letter of magazine

explanation.surface: A biased news item runs at the back of a magazine column.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Column' looks like a newspaper column; here it is the spinal column.
explanation.definitionFit: An anatomical sense of 'column': the vertebral column, stacked bones running down the back.

clue.text: Novice to shower wearing shirt

indicators.note: the shower is worn inside the shirt

blocks.note: a tee shirt; this is the outer word
a shower of rain; placed inside T…EE

explanation.surface: A beginner is told to shower with their shirt still on.
explanation.walkthrough: The shower is weather, not a bathroom, and the shirt wears it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both name a beginner still learning a job.

clue.text: Piano, late alternative for leader of singing

blocks.note: p = piano, soft, in music
the late news is the recent news
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: A choir hears that the piano is late and a stand-in must lead them.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all music, so 'Piano' reads as the instrument; it is the dynamic marking p.
explanation.definitionFit: A precentor leads the singing in a church or synagogue.

clue.text: Digression as man interrupts two relatives

indicators.note: the man breaks into the relatives

blocks.note: the first relative, with SIS the outer pair
he = a man; placed between the two relatives
sis = sister, the second relative

explanation.surface: A family conversation goes off-topic when a man cuts in.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface fits: a parenthesis is itself an interruption, the man breaking in just as a bracketed aside does.
explanation.definitionFit: A parenthesis is an aside or digression inserted into a passage.

clue.text: Refuse to deal with brawl: I had come in time for a bargain

indicators.note: I'D comes inside the brawl

blocks.note: to black goods is to boycott them, as a union might
a fray is a fight; the outer word
I'd = I had; placed inside FR…AY

explanation.surface: A shop worker refuses to deal with a fight that broke out in the sales rush.
explanation.walkthrough: To black something is British trade-union language for refusing to handle it; Black Friday is the day of sales after US Thanksgiving.
explanation.definitionFit: Black Friday is the post-Thanksgiving shopping day famous for bargains.
